title: Variables
intro: Variables are declared with `let`. They cannot change unless you add `mut`.

coming_from.go: `let` is your `:=`, but the variable can't change unless you write `let mut`. Writing `let count = ...` again in the same scope is allowed and makes a new variable, where Go's `:=` would complain that nothing is new.
coming_from.kotlin: `let` is your `val` and `let mut` is your `var`, and `let` also freezes the contents: a `val` list still takes `add`, a Rust `let` list does not take `push`. The other difference is shadowing: you can write `let count = ...` again in the same scope, even with a new type, which Kotlin won't allow.
coming_from.python: Any Python name can be reassigned, but a Rust `let` can't change unless you write `let mut`. Writing `let count = ...` again makes a new variable, and its type is still checked at compile time.
coming_from.typescript: Rust's `let` is your `const` and `let mut` is your `let`. Unlike `const`, a plain `let` also stops you changing what's inside (pushing to a `Vec`, setting a field), and you may redeclare the same name in one scope. (References and `Cell`-style types are the exceptions; the page covers them.)
coming_from.java: Rust flips Java's default: `let` is `final var`, and you add `mut` to get a plain changeable local. Rust's `let` also freezes the contents, where a `final` list still takes `add`. Rust also lets you shadow a name with a new `let`, which Java forbids for locals.
coming_from.csharp: `let` is a local you cannot reassign, which C# has no keyword for (`const` only works for compile-time constants, and locals can't be `readonly`). `let mut` is your everyday `var`, and a second `let` with the same name shadows the first, which C# rejects.
coming_from.c: `let` is `const int`, and `let mut` is a plain `int`, so the default is the reverse of C. Shadowing is allowed even in the same block, where C would report a redeclaration.
coming_from.cpp: `let x` is like `const auto x`, and `let mut x` like plain `auto x`, so Rust makes `const` the default. The difference: `auto` reads only the right-hand side, and `let` can wait for a later line to decide the type. Shadowing with a second `let` is allowed in the same scope, which C++ only allows in an inner block.

notes: Plain `let` can't change. You opt in with `let mut`, so a reader can see at a glance which variables change.
Shadowing (`let count = ...` again) makes a new variable that hides the old one. It can even have a different type. It is common for steps like `let input = input.trim();`.
`const` is for a value known before the program runs. It always needs a type and may sit outside any function, and by convention its name is `SHOUTING_CASE`.
A variable you never read gets a compiler warning. Start its name with `_` to say that is on purpose.

gotcha.title: Changing a variable without mut
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `count := 1` can always be changed later. (Kotlin refuses this too if you wrote `val`.)
gotcha.rust_sees: In Rust, plain `let` means "this never changes". You only get a changeable variable when you ask for one with `mut`.
gotcha.why: Rust chose this default so that a reader can see which variables change. The Rust Book's reason: code that assumes a value never changes can break when other code changes it. When you read `let x`, that name is not assigned again; only the `mut` ones need watching.

go.says: Go runs this and prints 2. A variable made with `:=` can always be changed later.
go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	count := 1
	count += 1
	fmt.Println(count)
}

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too if you write `val count = 1`; with `var` it runs and prints 2. Rust's `let` is Kotlin's `val`, and `let mut` is `var`. What is new is that Rust's `let` also stops the `push` on a list, as the page shows.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:3:5: error: 'val' cannot be reassigned.
    count += 1
    ^^^^^

python.says: Python has no `mut`: every variable can be reassigned, so this mistake can't happen.

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses this too if you write `const`: you cannot assign to a constant. Rust's `let` is TypeScript's `const`, and `let mut` is `let`.
typescript.error: main.ts(2,1): error TS2588: Cannot assign to 'count' because it is a constant.

java.says: Java locals can change by default, so this prints 2. Write `final var count = 1` and javac refuses it, like Rust's `let`.

csharp.says: A plain `var` can always change in C#, so this prints 2. Only `const` and `readonly` fields are locked, and local variables can't be `readonly`.

c.says: C variables can change unless you mark them `const`, so this prints 2. Rust flips the default: you opt in to change with `mut`.

cpp.says: C++ variables can change unless you mark them `const`, so this prints 2. Rust flips the default: you opt in to change with `mut`.

gotcha.error:
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `count`
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
2 |     let count = 1;
  |         ----- first assignment to `count`
3 |     count += 1;
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
  |
help: consider making this binding mutable
  |
2 |     let mut count = 1;
  |         +++

go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name := "gopher"
	count := 1
	count += 1
	count = count * 10
	fmt.Println(name, count)
}

kotlin.code:
fun main() {
    val name = "gopher"
    var count = 1
    count += 1
    count = count * 10
    println("$name $count")
}

python.code:
name = "gopher"
count = 1
count += 1

count = count * 10  # Python just reassigns; there is no separate "shadowing"
print(f"{name} {count}")
